paper_metadata.title: A 12.5Gb/s CMOS BER Test Using a Jitter-Tolerant Parallel CDR Yusuke Ohtomo, Tomoaki Kawamura, Kazuyoshi Nishimura, Masafumi Nogawa, Hiroshi Koizumi, Minoru Togashi

figures.label: Fig. 9
figures.caption: Figure 9.5.6 shows the CDR monitor outputs at 12.5Gb/s operation. Jitter characteristics of the parallel CDR are evaluated at the data rate of 10.66Gb/s. Jitter transfer measurement shows -3dB bandwidth of 4MHz and maximum jitter transfer peaking of less than 0.1dB. The measured jitter tolerance (Fig. 9.5.6) exceeds not only the SONET OC-192 jitter tolerance but also the XFP non-data-dependent jitter tolerance. The minimum jitter tolerance for (4-80MHz) sinusoidal jitter exceeds 0.5UIpp (jitter analyzer limit). Acknowledgements: The authors thank Y. Arai, Y. Kitamura and N. Tanaka for the fruitful discussions. References: [1] C. Hogge, “A Self-Correcting Clock Recovery Circuit,” J. Lightwave Technology, vol. LT-3, pp. 1312-1314, Dec. 1985. [2] J. Savoj, B. Razavi, “ A 10-Gb/s CMOS Clock and Data Recovery Circuit with a Half-Rate Linear Phase Detector,” IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits, vol. 36, pp. 761-768, May 2001. [3] J. Lee, B. Razavi, “A 40-Gb/s Clock and Data Recovery Circuit in 0.18µm CMOS Technology,” ISSCC Dig. Tech. Papers, pp. 242-245, Feb 2003.

references.sentence: This paper describes a CMOS LSI integrating PPG and BERT functions (Fig. 9.5.1).
To extend up-pulse width, we use a parallel phase detector (P-PD) and two chargepump (CP) circuits in a double-loop architecture CDR (Fig. 9.5.2).
The P-PD is shown in Fig. 9.5.3.

As shown in Fig. 9.5.4, a backannotated simulation at 11.1Gb/s indicates that the P-PD improves the linear response range to phase error from 0.33 to 0.56UI, suggesting that the minimum jitter tolerance would exceed 0.5UIpp. The parallel phase detector outputs an up-pulse that is 5/4-times wider than the down-pulse when phase error becomes zero.
Shunt-peaking and capacitance-coupling techniques are used for latches and XOR gates (Fig. 9.5.5) to accurately detect phase error and to divide 12.5GHz clock in half.
Figure 9.5.7 shows a micrograph of the chip.
Figure 9.5.6 shows the CDR monitor outputs at 12.5Gb/s operation.
The measured jitter tolerance (Fig. 9.5.6) exceeds not only the SONET OC-192 jitter tolerance but also the XFP non-data-dependent jitter tolerance.
